questions.prompt: In the titration, 50 mL of acid needed 50 mL of base to be neutral. What happens if you add 55 mL?
questions.explain: Extra base beyond the end point makes the solution basic.

questions.prompt: Why do chemists add the last few drops very slowly in a titration?
options: Near the end point one drop can change the pH sharply, so it's easy to overshoot
questions.explain: The pH jumps suddenly at the end point, so precise control is needed.

questions.prompt: Which are BASES used to neutralise acids? Choose all that apply.
questions.explain: Vinegar and lemon juice are acids.

options: any compound formed when an acid reacts with a base
questions.explain: There are many salts: sodium chloride, calcium sulfate, potassium nitrate, and more.

questions.prompt: Put the titration steps in order.
steps: Measure 50 mL of acid into a flask
Add a few drops of indicator
Add base, swirling, until the indicator just changes colour
Record the volume of base used
questions.explain: Measure acid → indicator → fill burette → titrate to end point → record.

questions.prompt: Explain why taking too many antacid tablets could be a problem.
questions.modelAnswer: Antacids are bases. Taking too many would neutralise too much stomach acid and could make the stomach contents less acidic than needed. Stomach acid is needed to digest food and kill germs, so digestion could suffer.
rubric: Antacids are bases that neutralise acid
Too much could over-neutralise / make it basic
Stomach acid is needed for digestion or killing germs
questions.explain: Balance matters: the right amount of base, not the most.
